description: A HAVING predicate must decide which rows a page contains, not which of an already-chosen page survives. Ordering by name takes a shortcut the other orderings have no equivalent for: it walks the name index in order and stops once it holds LIMIT rows. That is correct only while every filter has already run. HAVING runs after the page is cut, so while the shortcut was allowed to fire alongside one, the answer was the first LIMIT rows by name minus those failing HAVING instead of the first LIMIT rows by name that satisfy it -- rows that qualify were never fetched, nothing was truncated in the reply, and no error was raised. The name-ordered fast paths and the running top-K trim are now all gated on HAVING being absent, and these cases hold them to it. The pairs below differ in one keyword at a time so a regression cannot be misattributed: WHERE against HAVING at the same limit, and name-ordering against orderings that materialise before paging.

cases.name: the_answer_this_suite_measures_against
cases.description: Ground truth, ordered by a field with no index shortcut so the full candidate set is materialised and HAVING runs before the limit. Seven functions in this corpus exceed 150 lines. Every case below asks for those same seven, or a prefix of them. This case also shares the corpus with the expected failures, so an unregistered corpus cannot pass itself off as the defect.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 1001

cases.name: a_where_predicate_survives_the_name_ordered_page
cases.description: The control that isolates the keyword. Identical to the case below in every character except WHERE for HAVING. A WHERE predicate filters rows as they are scanned, so the shortcut collects three rows that satisfy it and the answer is right. Keep this passing: if it ever fails, the fault has moved out of HAVING and the case below is no longer measuring what it claims.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 3

cases.name: an_unordered_page_is_chosen_by_the_predicate_too
cases.description: The same page with no ORDER BY at all. Ordering by name was not the only early exit: with no ORDER BY and no GROUP BY the scan used to stop opening segments once it held LIMIT + 1 rows, and HAVING was applied to those, so the shape failed the same way for a different reason. That cap is gone -- a HAVING now disarms the running trim as well, so every matching row is materialised and the predicate sees all of them. Rows come back in the default (name, line, path, fql_kind) order, so the same three qualify. A limit far above the answer truncated it here too -- seven rows came back as two.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 LIMIT 3

cases.name: a_having_predicate_survives_the_name_ordered_page
cases.description: The same three rows, asked for with HAVING instead of WHERE. A page of three is requested and three qualifying rows exist, so three must come back. While the shortcut was ungated it took the first three functions by name -- none of which is long enough -- applied HAVING to those, and returned nothing at all. This case needs both halves of the fix: gating the name shortcut sends it to the pipeline, where the running top-K trim sheds by name before HAVING runs and would answer nothing just the same, so the trim is gated on HAVING too.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 3

cases.name: a_limit_larger_than_the_answer_still_returns_all_of_it
cases.description: A limit far above the seven matching rows cannot bound the answer, so all seven must come back whatever the ordering. While the shortcut was ungated only three did -- the ones whose names fell inside the window it stopped at; the other four sort later in the alphabet and were never looked at. This limit is above the top-K trim's threshold, so the trim never armed here and the shortcut alone accounts for the loss.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 1001

cases.name: reversing_the_order_does_not_change_which_rows_qualify
cases.description: The direction of an ORDER BY decides the sequence rows come back in, never which rows are in the answer. Descending must return the same seven as ascending. While the shortcut was ungated it returned one -- the single qualifying name that falls inside the window when the walk runs from the other end, which was the clearest statement that the window and not the predicate was choosing the answer.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' HAVING lines > 150 ORDER BY name DESC LIMIT 1001
